title: Investigating Habituation to Premonitory Urges in Behavior Therapy for Tic Disorders.

publication_date_precision: day as primary bibliographic metadata reports
reviewer: AI-assisted bounded primary-source audit; not clinical peer review
evidence_type: Historical secondary mechanism analysis of two randomized treatment-package trials
population: Youth 9–17 and older trial starting at age 16; moderate or greater tics, clinical-stability restrictions

sample.model_specific_n: Do not substitute original randomized counts for analyzed denominators

assignment: CBIT versus psychoeducation/supportive therapy, matched therapist time; mediator not randomized
counterevidence: Older CBIT responders showed a declining-urge pattern, but not a specific established treatment-induced mediator; youth did not show significant global urge change.
limitations: Concurrent change-score intervals do not ensure mediator precedes outcome.

title: Bothersome tics in patients with chronic tic disorders: Characteristics and individualized treatment response to behavior therapy.
authors: McGuire JF, Piacentini J, Scahill L, Woods DW, Villarreal R, Wilhelm S, Walkup JT, Peterson AL.
publication_date_precision: day as primary bibliographic metadata reports
reviewer: AI-assisted bounded primary-source audit; not clinical peer review
evidence_type: Historical secondary treatment-moderator analysis of two randomized trials
population: Children and adults; selected clinically stable original CBIT cohorts
assignment: Whole CBIT versus supportive therapy; baseline urge presence not randomized
measurement: Bothersome tics nominated at baseline; posttreatment severity

results.p_consistency_note: Reported F and degrees of freedom imply approximately.01823, inconsistent with the printed p<.015. Preserve both without repairing the paper; not a participant-data reanalysis.

claim_supported: A baseline tic-characteristic moderation signal, with package benefit in both reported urge groups.
claim_not_supported: A component-selection rule, untrained-tic effect, independent replication, validated personalized strategy or cure
limitations: Exact training target and timing absent.
Complete treatment-data subset; multiple tic-level comparisons.

Methods describe tic-level ANCOVA and Sidak pairwise comparisons, with no participant-cluster correction described. Within-person dependence and reported precision remain concerns; no reconstructed confidence intervals.
Main methods describe 207 complete participants relative to 248; do not subtract 41 from 240 and substitute 199.
access: Full author-manuscript selected methods/results/limitations via NCBI BioC and indexed PMC; no raw data.

title: Working Mechanisms of Exposure and Response Prevention in the Treatment of Tourette Syndrome and Tic Disorders Revisited: No Evidence for within-Session Habituation to Premonitory Urges.
authors: van de Griendt JMTM, van den Berg NME, Verdellen CWJ, Cath DC, Verbraak MJPM.
publication_date_precision: day as primary bibliographic metadata reports
reviewer: AI-assisted bounded primary-source audit; not clinical peer review
population: 29 participants ages 7–59; relatively mild tics, selected outpatient sample
assignment: No randomized mechanism contrast in this analysis
measurement: Twelve weekly one-hour visits: two training visits plus ten measured ERP sessions; urge ratings at 0, 5, 10, 15, 30, 45 and 60 minutes; sessions pooled for trajectory modeling

results.observed_pattern: Urges increased in first 15 minutes then remained elevated; no demonstrated within-session habituation.
results.fit_note: Best fit relative to tested alternatives, but poor absolute fit; not a validated trajectory model.
results.YGTSS_source_note: Cohort change cited in article from original 2018 report, not a new randomized estimate.

claim_supported: Clinical improvement can coexist with a group urge trajectory lacking within-session reduction in this selected cohort.
claim_not_supported: Within-session causal mediation, between-session habituation absent, duration equivalence, adult-severe generalization or alternative mechanism proven
limitations: No YGTSS at every session.
Urge-rating attention/frequency may alter ratings.
Group/session averaging may mask heterogeneity; piecewise model absolute fit remains poor despite the best relative fit.
Repeated observations do not create more independent participants.
harms: Not a systematic new harms study.
funding_conflicts: Authors declare no conflicts of interest and state that listed current employers were not involved. This is an author declaration, not independent clearance. Funding not established in the inspected sections.
access: Full text via EuropePMC XML and indexed PMC; no participant tables or data files retained.

population: Original youth and older CBIT trial cohorts
measurement: New bothersome tics at weeks 5/10, adverse-event monitoring, medication changes and selected comorbidity measures

results.new_bothersome_tic_occurrence: No demonstrated between-arm increase with CBIT over ten weeks; no equivalence or exhaustive all-tic detection conclusion.

claim_supported: Controlled evidence challenges a general symptom-substitution concern for recorded new bothersome tics during the ten-week treatment window.
claim_not_supported: Positive untreated-tic transfer, no harm in every subgroup, long-term function or cure
harms: Structured visit questioning allowed spontaneous reports regardless of attributed cause; rare/delayed/effort-related harms not excluded.
limitations: Same cohorts as Houghton/McGuire; not independent replication.
Usable-data selection, ten-week primary window and ascertainment of bothersome tics rather than exhaustive detection of all new tics.
Adult event totals in narrative are internally inconsistent; not combined or repaired in this audit.
